clinicalPearls: Hydroxyapatite deposition disease (HADD) is caused by deposition of hydroxyapatite, a basic calcium phosphate crystal, within tendons, bursae, and other periarticular soft tissues

Its best-known form is calcific tendinitis, most frequently affecting the rotator cuff (especially the supraspinatus) at the shoulder, but also the hip, elbow, wrist, and around the spine (for example longus colli tendinitis)
Patients may be asymptomatic, have a chronic ache, or suffer acute attacks of severe pain when a deposit becomes inflamed or ruptures into an adjacent bursa during the resorptive phase
Radiographs show rounded or cloud-like calcific deposits within tendons whose appearance evolves through formative and resorptive phases, and deposits may disappear over time
It commonly presents in middle age, can be bilateral, and must be distinguished from an avulsion fracture and from tumoral calcinosis
The crystals are non-birefringent and not seen on standard polarised microscopy, so the diagnosis is largely clinical and radiological
Management is symptomatic, using rest, anti-inflammatory therapy, physiotherapy, and ultrasound-guided needling (barbotage) or aspiration, with surgery reserved for refractory deposits
reference.pathophysiology: Hydroxyapatite crystals are deposited within tendons and periarticular soft tissue, often at sites of relative hypovascularity or altered cell metabolism such as the rotator cuff. The disease progresses through phases: a quiescent formative phase of crystal accumulation followed by a resorptive phase in which the deposit becomes vascularised and crystals are shed, provoking intense inflammation and acute pain. Rupture of a deposit into a neighbouring bursa produces acute calcific bursitis. Over time deposits may resorb completely, which is why the radiographic appearance changes and symptoms often ultimately settle.
additionalDifferentials: Tumoral calcinosis or soft-tissue calcification from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs to identify and stage the calcific deposits
Ultrasound to characterise deposits and to guide barbotage or aspiration
MRI for associated rotator cuff pathology or when the diagnosis is unclear
Aspiration and analysis of bursal fluid with culture to exclude infection during acute attacks
Alizarin red staining to suggest calcium-containing crystals, which are non-birefringent on polarised light
Cross-sectional CT for deep or atypical sites such as retropharyngeal longus colli tendinitis
redFlags: Acute severe pain with fever mimicking septic arthritis or bursitis
Retropharyngeal (longus colli) calcific tendinitis presenting with acute neck pain and dysphagia
Rapidly destructive joint changes suggesting a BCP-related destructive arthropathy
reference.prognosis: The natural history is often favourable, with acute episodes settling and deposits frequently resorbing spontaneously; most patients recover with conservative treatment, although some experience recurrent or persistent symptoms requiring intervention.
pitfalls: Mistaking a periarticular calcific deposit for an avulsion fracture
Treating self-limiting acute calcific tendinitis as infection
Failing to recognise atypical sites such as retropharyngeal longus colli tendinitis
Expecting polarised microscopy to reveal the non-birefringent crystals
management: Conservative management of acute calcific tendinitis with rest, analgesia, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Physiotherapy to restore range of movement and function
Ultrasound-guided barbotage (needle aspiration and lavage) of symptomatic deposits
Local corticosteroid injection into the subacromial space or affected bursa for persistent pain
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for chronic or resistant deposits
Arthroscopic or surgical removal of the deposit for refractory disease
Aspiration and culture to exclude septic bursitis during a severe acute attack
Reassurance that the natural history is often self-limiting with spontaneous resorption of deposits
